processing: A green tea taken through ten steps: fixing, first rolling, pan-firing, second rolling, first baking, shaping, second baking, raising the down, full drying and a final baking for aroma.
harvest_season: Usually picked before Qingming. One bud with a just-opening leaf makes the first grade; one bud with two young leaves makes the second.
appearance_dry: Round, tight, plump strands of even size, bright green with plenty of white down.
appearance_wet: Plump, whole, tender leaves of a bright young green.
taste_profile: Fresh and mellow with a lasting young-leaf aroma and a sweet return in the throat.

brewing.notes: General practice for a downy spring green tea rather than a rule specific to this one: use water well off the boil and expect a little haze from the down.

vintage_note: Sold like other Chinese spring greens, as the current year's harvest, with pre-Qingming picking the prized part. It is meant for drinking fresh, not ageing. Ask for the picking standard, since it decides the grade.
description:
Ziyang Maojian is the best-known named green tea of Ziyang county in southern Shaanxi, grown in the valleys on the upper Han River at the northern foot of the Daba Mountains. This is a northerly place for tea in China, which is part of its local pride. The tea is sold as part of the wider Ziyang selenium tea family.

The leaf comes from local bushes with fat, very downy buds, the Ziyang Zhong and Ziyang Dayepao varieties. A long ten-step process alternates rolling, firing and baking, with a separate step to bring the down to the surface. The result is a round, tight strand that looks frosted with white hairs.

Expect a mellow, fresh cup with a young-leaf aroma and a sweet finish. As with other downy green teas, the liquor may look slightly hazy at first, and that is the hair rather than a fault. Scalding water is the usual way to flatten a tea like this, so let the kettle cool.

Buy it fresh and ask about the picking. Selenium content is the headline in much of the selling, along with health claims that go well beyond what a cup of tea can promise, so judge the leaf by its look and smell first.
history:
Ziyang Maojian is called a historic tea, and Chinese popular accounts link it to tea buds sent as tribute under the Tang and to praise in the county gazetteer, which compared it to a pearl of the black dragon. These stories are repeated more often than they are documented, so treat the details with care.

Its modern reputation rests on selenium: research on Ziyang tea from the late 1970s and early 1980s drew attention to the county's selenium-rich soils. Maojian has a registered geographical-indication trademark.
